asDecan.p: Your Sun sits between 20 and 29 degrees of Capricorn, the last third of the sign. Each ten-degree slice of a sign is a decan with its own planet and card, and in the Chaldean order this one goes to the Sun. The Sun has no special dignity in Capricorn. It's a visitor there, neither helped nor held back, so it takes on the colour of Saturn, who rules the sign. The Sun is the part of a chart that wants to be somebody, and here that gets tied to what you've built and kept. The Two of Pentacles, Jupiter's decan, is the juggler at the start of the sign, and the Three, which Mars has, is the craftsman on the job. By your slice the building's mostly done, and the question is what to keep. The man in the picture has a coin on his head, one clutched to his chest and two under his boots, and he isn't getting up. The Devil is your Sun card, and this is the finer grain inside it.

You know roughly what's in your bank account at any given moment, and you'd be a bit embarrassed to say how often you check. At a restaurant with friends, when someone suggests splitting the bill evenly, you do a quick sum in your head about who had the wine, and mostly you say nothing. A Sunday with nothing planned tends to turn into a Sunday sorting something out, the spare room, the tax folder, the spreadsheet for the house. You lend your good tools reluctantly and you notice when they come back late. None of this is meanness, and the people who know you well can see that. The Sun here wants to be proud of something solid, and Saturn has taught it that solid things go missing when nobody's watching. So you keep watch, and most of the time you don't even notice you're doing it.

Other people's things end up with you. The family photos live at your place. You're the one asked to be treasurer of the tennis club, to hold the spare key, to be executor of an aunt's will, and it's because everyone can tell that what goes into your hands comes back out in better shape. When your grandmother's recipe book was falling apart, you were the one who had it rebound. The Sun likes being trusted with something that matters, and Saturn makes sure you don't drop it. You're also usually right about what things are worth. Haggling over a second-hand car or asking for a pay rise, you know the fair number and you hold it calmly, without getting heated, and the person across the table tends to remember that about you long after the deal's done.

Once you've put years into something, a job, a house, a way of doing the accounts at work, walking away feels like admitting the years were wasted, so you stay. From the outside it looks like loyalty. I see this a lot with late Capricorn Suns. The house that's been too big since the kids left, kept because it's paid off. The role that stopped growing five years ago. There's pride tangled up in it, because in these degrees the Sun measures you by what you've gathered, and giving any of it up feels like getting smaller. It turns up in small ways too. An argument from a family Christmas gets kept on file for years and brought out exactly when it helps your case.

When something goes wrong, a job cut, a break-up, a big bill nobody saw coming, your first move is to batten down. You cancel the subscriptions, stop going out, go through the accounts line by line and tell everyone you're fine. That part is often useful, to be honest. About a week later the battening has spread. You've stopped answering messages, you're working late for no clear reason, and you've gone quiet at home in a way that's hard to live next to. Your partner or your kids can feel the lid on, and they tend to take it personally. Saturn's instinct is to carry the whole thing alone. What helps is letting one person see the actual numbers, the real size of the problem, whatever it is. Once someone else has seen it, you usually loosen up enough to sleep.

You show love by providing, and by keeping things. The ticket from a first date is still in a drawer twenty years later, and you know which drawer. What's less obvious is how awkward you are on the receiving end. An expensive present from someone new makes you uneasy, as if you now owe them, and you'll quietly work out how to even it up. Being looked after when you're sick is almost worse. The Devil, your Sun card, is about ties that are hard to undo, and once you've committed to someone you're very slow to leave, though it takes a long while before anyone's given a key to your place. The partners who suit you are patient, reasonably settled in their own finances, and happy to let you run the household money for a year or two before they ask to see the books.

You're built for work where something has to be looked after over a long stretch. Finance, property, a family business, a museum collection or a pension fund, the operations side of any place that can't afford to lose things. The Three of Pentacles people, one decan back, love the craft of the job itself. You care about what the job adds up to over ten years, and the Sun in you wants a title you've earned and a desk that's properly yours. Where it goes wrong is handing things over. You'll keep doing the budget yourself long after you've got a team, because giving it away means trusting someone else with what you've guarded. So the team never learns how, you can't take a proper holiday, and when you do, you check the shared inbox from the beach.

At twenty this decan can seem old for its age. Saving hard, living carefully, a bit judgemental about friends who spend their wages on a trip to Bali. There's often a family story behind it, a lean patch or a parent who worried about money out loud. By the mid-thirties most people with a Sun here have built something real, a deposit, a position, some standing, and the work becomes deciding how much of it needs guarding. That's usually when the first hard lesson about holding too tight arrives, a friendship or a relationship that went cold from it. These degrees sit at the end of Capricorn, already leaning toward Aquarius, and the fifties often bring that side out. People start giving on purpose, backing a nephew's first business, paying for the community garden, handing the good tools on to someone younger who'll use them.

Once a month, give away something you'd normally keep. It doesn't have to be money. A book you'll never reread, handed to someone who'd like it. An afternoon of your weekend helping a friend move house. The good bottle you were saving for an occasion, opened on an ordinary Wednesday with whoever's around. Write one line about what you gave and how it felt the next day. After six months, read the list back to yourself.
